options.text: A block of code that you can pass around and store in constants or variables.
options.explanation: Right. Closures are code blocks that you can store in variables or pass to functions.

options.text: A special struct that can only hold static properties and methods with no functions.
options.explanation: Closures are blocks of code that run, not static structs.

options.text: A Swift struct that copies all values every time you pass it to a function.
options.explanation: Closures are reference types, not value-type structs.

options.text: A memory pointer where you must free memory by hand after it finishes.
options.explanation: Swift manages closure memory for you.

questions.prompt: What does the in keyword do inside a Swift closure expression?

options.text: It imports another Swift module into the closure.
options.explanation: Modules are imported with the import keyword.

options.text: It separates the parameter list and return type from the closure body.
options.explanation: Right. The in keyword marks where the body statements begin.

options.text: It starts a loop that steps through each item in a collection.
options.explanation: A for-in loop uses in, but inside a closure it separates parameters from the body.

options.text: It repeats the closure body once for each parameter.
options.explanation: The in keyword does not repeat code; it separates parameters from the body.

questions.prompt: Are closures and functions in Swift value types or reference types?

options.text: They are value types that make separate copies when you assign them.
options.explanation: Closures are not value types.

options.text: They are value types at the top level, but reference types inside classes.
options.explanation: All closures and functions are reference types everywhere in Swift.

options.text: They are reference types, so assigning a closure shares the same closure and state.
options.explanation: Right. Closures are reference types and share captured values.

options.text: They are simple numbers that only live while a single line runs.
options.explanation: Closures are reference types that can stay alive and keep captured values.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes how functions and closures relate in Swift?

options.text: Functions and closures are different types that can never share a parameter list.
options.explanation: Functions and closures can have the exact same function type.

options.text: Closures are value types, while functions are reference types.
options.explanation: Both functions and closures are reference types.

options.text: Closures cannot take parameters or return values, while functions can.
options.explanation: Closures can take parameters and return values just like functions.

options.text: Functions are special cases of closures that have a name.
options.explanation: Right. Global and nested functions are named closures.

questions.prompt: What is trailing closure syntax in Swift?

options.text: Writing a closure expression after the function call parentheses when it is the last argument.
options.explanation: Right. Trailing closure syntax places the closure block after the parentheses.

options.text: Putting a closure parameter at the start of a function parameter list.
options.explanation: Trailing closures go at the end of the call, not the start.

options.text: Running a closure after a timer finishes counting down.
options.explanation: Trailing closure is a syntax shortcut, not a timer.

options.text: Adding a semicolon at the end of a closure body.
options.explanation: Swift does not use semicolons for trailing closures.

questions.prompt: When can you leave out the empty parentheses () completely when calling a function with a trailing closure?

options.text: Only when the closure returns Void.
options.explanation: The return type does not decide whether you can drop the parentheses.

options.text: When the closure is the only argument the function takes.
options.explanation: Right. When the closure is the only argument, you do not need empty parentheses.

options.text: Whenever the closure uses shorthand argument names like $0.
options.explanation: You can drop empty parentheses based on the argument count, not shorthand names.

options.text: Never, because function call parentheses are always required.
options.explanation: Swift lets you leave out empty parentheses when the closure is the only argument.

questions.prompt: What happens if you use $0 inside a closure that also lists named parameters?

options.text: The closure treats $0 as the return value instead of an argument.
options.explanation: Shorthand names stand for arguments, not return values.

options.text: The code runs normally because Swift links parameter names to $0.
options.explanation: Swift does not allow mixing named parameters with $0.

options.text: The compiler gives an error because you cannot mix $0 and named parameters.

options.text: The first parameter gets a default value of zero.
options.explanation: Shorthand names do not give default values.

questions.prompt: What do the shorthand names $0 and $1 stand for inside a closure body?

options.text: The first two items stored inside an array variable.
options.explanation: $0 and $1 refer to the closure arguments, not array items.

options.text: Global constants declared outside the closure body.
options.explanation: They refer to the arguments passed into the closure.

options.text: The closure return value and any thrown error.
options.explanation: They stand for input arguments by position, starting at zero.

options.text: The first and second arguments passed to the closure.
options.explanation: Right. $0 is the first argument, $1 is the second, and so on.

questions.prompt: When you use shorthand argument names like $0 and $1, what else can you leave out of the closure?

options.text: The parameter list and the in keyword.
options.explanation: Right. With shorthand names, you leave out the parameters and the in keyword.

options.text: The curly braces around the closure body.
options.explanation: Curly braces are always needed around a closure.

options.text: The code statements inside the closure body.
options.explanation: The closure still needs body code to compute a result.

options.text: The name of the function you are calling.
options.explanation: You still write the function name when calling it.

questions.prompt: What does it mean when a closure captures a value from the function around it?

options.text: It locks the variable so no other function can read it.
options.explanation: Capturing does not lock a variable against other reads.

options.text: It keeps a reference to the variable so the closure can still use it after that scope ends.
options.explanation: Right. The captured variable stays alive in memory for the closure.

options.text: It makes a separate copy that resets to zero after each call.
options.explanation: Captured variables keep their updated values across calls.

options.text: It turns the variable into a constant that can never change again.
options.explanation: The closure can both read and update a captured var.

questions.prompt: When can a closure leave out the return keyword?

options.text: Only when the closure returns an optional value.
options.explanation: Optional return types do not decide if you can leave out return.

options.text: Only when the closure takes zero parameters.
options.explanation: Closures with any number of parameters can leave out return if they have one expression.

options.text: When the closure body has just one expression that gives the return value.
options.explanation: Right. Swift returns the result of a single-expression closure for you.

options.text: Whenever every parameter in the closure has an explicit type.
options.explanation: Parameter types do not decide implicit return; having one expression does.

questions.prompt: Which type of closure has a name and can capture values from the function around it?

options.text: A global function.
options.explanation: Global functions have names, but they do not capture values.

options.text: An inline closure expression.
options.explanation: Closure expressions do not have names.

options.text: An unnamed closure block.
options.explanation: Unnamed closures do not have a name.

options.text: A nested function.
options.explanation: Right. Nested functions are named closures that can capture values from the enclosing function.

options.text: It updates the same captured counter shared with firstClosure.

options.text: It creates a separate copy with a new counter starting at zero.

options.text: It crashes at runtime because two constants point to one closure.
options.explanation: Calling shared closures one after another works safely in Swift.

options.text: It resets the captured counter back to its starting value.
options.explanation: Calling a closure does not reset captured variables.

options.text: Because sorted(by:) turns all items into Any before running the closure.

options.text: Because the Swift compiler ignores type rules inside curly braces.
options.explanation: The compiler checks types strictly inside closures.

questions.prompt: Which closure expression uses the cleanest short Swift syntax to sort numbers from highest to lowest?

options.text: numbers.sorted(by: { (a: Int, b: Int) -> Bool in return a > b })
options.explanation: This compiles, but the types, labels, and return keyword are not needed.

options.text: numbers.sorted(by: { a, b in return a > b })
options.explanation: This skips types, but it still uses named parameters and return.

options.text: numbers.sorted { $0 > $1 }
options.explanation: Right. It uses a trailing closure, shorthand names, implicit return, and no empty parentheses.

options.text: numbers.sorted() { (a, b) in a > b }
options.explanation: The empty parentheses and parameter names are unnecessary.

questions.prompt: What is a closure in Swift, and how does it relate to a function? Answer in 2–5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: In Swift, a closure is a block of code that you can store in a variable and pass to functions. Functions are special named closures. Global functions have names and do not capture values, while nested functions have names and can capture values. Closure expressions are unnamed blocks of code written inline.

rubric.criterion: Explains that a closure is a block of code that can be stored, passed around, and run
Explains that named functions are special cases of closures
Notes that closure expressions can be written inline with no function name

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the in keyword in a Swift closure expression? Answer in 2–5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: The in keyword separates the closure header from its body statements. You put the parameter list and return type before the in keyword. The code statements that run go right after the in keyword. When you use shorthand names like $0, you can leave out the parameter list and the in keyword.

rubric.criterion: Explains that in separates the closure parameters and return type from the body
States that the parameter list and return type come before in
Notes that the closure body code comes after in

questions.prompt: Explain value capturing in Swift closures. What happens to a captured local variable after its enclosing function finishes? Answer in 2–5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: Value capturing lets a closure use variables from the scope around it where it was created. Even after the enclosing function finishes running and returns, the captured variable stays alive in memory. The closure keeps a reference to that variable, so it can still read and update the value on later calls.

rubric.criterion: Explains that closures capture references to variables from the surrounding scope
States that captured variables stay alive in memory after the enclosing function returns
Mentions that the closure can still read or change the captured variable

questions.prompt: Are closures value types or reference types in Swift? What happens when you assign a closure to two constants or variables? Answer in 2–5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: Closures and functions in Swift are reference types, not value types. When you assign a closure to two constants or variables, both point to the exact same closure. They share any captured variables, so changing a captured value through one reference also changes it for the other.

rubric.criterion: Explains that closures and functions are reference types
States that assigning a closure to multiple variables makes them point to the same closure
Explains that captured state is shared across all references

questions.prompt: Explain trailing closure syntax in Swift. When can you leave out the function call parentheses completely? Answer in 2–5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: Trailing closure syntax lets you write a closure after the closing parenthesis when it is the final argument of a function. If the closure is the only argument the function takes, you can leave out the empty parentheses completely. This makes calls to functions like map, filter, and sorted short and easy to read.

rubric.criterion: Explains that trailing closures go outside the parentheses when the closure is the final argument
States that parentheses can be left out completely when the closure is the only argument
Notes that this keeps calls to functions like map and filter short and easy to read
